Confidence threshold is a brittle hyperparameter: a loose threshold injects noisy labels; a strict one starves the algorithm of unlabeled signal, degrading it toward pure supervised learning.
Assumes the base classifier is well-calibrated; overconfident models (e.g., uncalibrated neural networks) produce high-confidence wrong pseudo-labels that corrupt subsequent iterations.
recommended_for: NLP tasks with abundant unlabeled text and sparse manual annotations, such as word sense disambiguation or named-entity recognition, where a small seed set of labeled examples bootstraps the classifier.
Tabular classification with class-separable feature distributions (e.g., medical screening where positive and negative cases cluster distinctly), ensuring confident pseudo-labels are likely correct.
not_recommended_for: Highly imbalanced datasets where the minority class is chronically under-represented in confident predictions, causing Self-Training to collapse toward the majority class over iterations.
Tasks requiring calibrated probability outputs (e.g., risk scoring), since iterative retraining on pseudo-labels distorts the original probability estimates of the base model.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Yarowsky (1995) for unsupervised word sense disambiguation — achieving 96.5% accuracy on a binary sense task using only 12 labeled seed collocations — the algorithm predates the term 'semi-supervised learning' and was analyzed mathematically only a decade later by Abney (2004), who showed it approximately maximizes a Bregman-distance-based cross-entropy objective.

children.name: Co-Training
children.diff_siblings: Co-Training requires the feature space to be naturally partitioned into two conditionally independent and individually sufficient views, training a separate classifier on each view and iteratively labeling unlabeled data for the other — unlike self-training (single model bootstraps itself) or label propagation (graph-based diffusion with no classifier pair).
strengths: Reduces error reinforcement: two classifiers built on independent feature views must agree before a pseudo-label is adopted, so view-specific biases do not compound as they do in single-model self-training.

Exploits natural multi-view data with minimal labeled samples — web page classification using page text and anchor link text is a canonical case where each view alone is sufficient and the method yields near-supervised accuracy.

PAC-learnable guarantee: Blum and Mitchell (1998) proved that under the sufficient-and-redundant-views assumption, co-training converges with exponentially fewer labeled examples than a purely supervised approach.
weaknesses: Natural feature split is rarely available: most tabular and image datasets lack two conditionally independent sufficient views, forcing artificial splits that violate the theoretical assumptions and degrade performance.
Classifiers converge and saturate after several rounds as they learn from each other, reducing disagreement below the level needed to generate informative pseudo-labels.
Error amplification risk: if one classifier makes systematic mistakes early on, those pseudo-labels corrupt the other classifier's training set, and the error propagates irreversibly across rounds.
recommended_for: Multi-modal text datasets where two natural feature spaces exist independently — e.g., classifying scientific papers using both abstract words and citation-network features, with fewer than 1% of documents labeled.
Web-page categorization where HTML body text and hyperlink anchor text constitute two sufficient, largely independent feature views and labeled pages are scarce.
not_recommended_for: Single-view datasets (images, time series, standard tabular data) where any feature split creates two insufficient and correlated subsets, breaking the conditional-independence assumption the algorithm requires.
Domains where labeling errors are costly, since systematic mistakes by one view propagate irreversibly into the other classifier's training data with no built-in error-correction mechanism.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Avrim Blum and Tom Mitchell (1998) in 'Combining Labeled and Unlabeled Data with Co-Training' (COLT 1998), the method was validated on a web-page classification task where using anchor text and page text as two views allowed the algorithm to bootstrap from just 12 labeled pages to near-fully-supervised accuracy on 1,000+ unlabeled pages.
keywords: two classifiers labeling for each other
small labeled dataset large unlabeled dataset

children.name: Pseudo-Labels
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Label Propagation (which spreads labels via graph neighborhood structure) and Self-Training (which retrains iteratively on high-confidence predictions), Pseudo-Labels assigns hard class labels to unlabeled samples using the current network's argmax softmax output and trains on labeled and pseudo-labeled data jointly in every mini-batch, making the approach tightly coupled to deep neural network training loops.
strengths: Mathematically equivalent to entropy regularization: minimizing H(p(y|x)) on unlabeled data encourages low-density class boundaries without an explicit graph or density estimator.
Zero architectural overhead: requires no changes to the model, loss function structure, or optimizer — only a confidence threshold and a weighting schedule (e.g., T1/T2 ramp-up) are added.
Scales to large unlabeled corpora because pseudo-label assignment is O(N) per forward pass and adds no pairwise or graph computation.
weaknesses: Confirmation bias: early incorrect pseudo-labels are reinforced over successive epochs, compounding errors in a feedback loop that degrades final accuracy, especially when labeled data is scarce (< 1% of total).

Hard threshold sensitivity: a fixed confidence cutoff (e.g., 0.95 softmax max) either discards most unlabeled data early in training or admits noisy labels late — neither static value is optimal across the full training trajectory.
Assumes class balance: pseudo-label selection skews toward majority classes because their softmax scores are systematically higher, causing under-selection of minority classes in imbalanced datasets.
recommended_for: Image classification pipelines where a large unlabeled image corpus exists alongside a small labeled set (e.g., 250–4000 labels on CIFAR-10/ImageNet), and the base model already reaches >70% accuracy on labeled data before pseudo-labeling begins.

Any task where the labeled and unlabeled distributions are matched and a pre-trained backbone (e.g., ResNet, ViT) is fine-tuned, because high initial confidence reduces confirmation bias from the start.
not_recommended_for: Heavily class-imbalanced datasets (e.g., rare disease detection, fraud detection with <0.1% positives) where majority-class dominance in softmax scores systematically excludes minority-class unlabeled samples from pseudo-labeling.

Structured prediction tasks (sequence labeling, semantic segmentation at pixel level) where a single wrong pseudo-label on one token or pixel propagates strong gradient signal across the entire output, making error compounding faster and harder to detect.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Dong-Hyun Lee in a workshop paper at ICML 2013 ('Pseudo-Label: The Simple and Efficient Semi-Supervised Learning Method for Deep Neural Networks'), Lee proved that training with hard pseudo-labels is formally equivalent to entropy regularization — minimizing the conditional entropy H(p(y|x)) of the model's predictions on unlabeled data — a theoretical connection that later grounded an entire family of consistency-regularization methods including MixMatch and FixMatch.

children.name: TSVM (Transductive SVM)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike graph-based siblings (Label Propagation, Label Spreading) or iterative pseudo-label methods (Self-Training, Co-Training, Pseudo-Labels), TSVM extends the SVM max-margin objective directly to unlabeled points, solving a single non-convex mixed-integer optimization that forces the decision hyperplane into low-density regions for all data simultaneously.
strengths: Maximizes margin over labeled and unlabeled points jointly, giving the tightest theoretical generalization bound among the semi-supervised siblings under the SVM framework.

Particularly effective with very small labeled sets (Joachims 1999 showed cutting required labels to 1/20th on text tasks) because the max-margin constraint leverages unlabeled structure aggressively.
Produces a sparse support-vector solution identical in form to a standard SVM, making the resulting classifier interpretable and compatible with kernel methods.
weaknesses: The joint optimization is non-convex (NP-hard in the general case); practical solvers use iterative label-switching heuristics that are sensitive to initialization and offer no global optimality guarantee.
Scales as O(n^3) in memory and time with the number of unlabeled points due to kernel matrix storage, making it impractical beyond ~10,000 samples without approximations.
Assumes the low-density separation hypothesis holds; when class boundaries pass through dense regions, unlabeled data can actively degrade accuracy compared to a plain supervised SVM.
recommended_for: Text classification with very few labeled documents (e.g., fewer than 100 labels among thousands of unlabeled articles), where the bag-of-words kernel aligns well with the low-density assumption.

Biomedical binary classification (e.g., disease vs. control) with expensive annotation but abundant raw assay data, where a kernel can encode domain similarity and the class boundary is expected to lie in a sparse region.
not_recommended_for: Datasets with more than ~10,000 unlabeled points, where the O(n^3) kernel matrix makes training memory-prohibitive without approximations that undermine the margin guarantee.

Multi-class problems or scenarios requiring online prediction for new test points not seen during training, since the classic TSVM optimizes over a fixed unlabeled set and does not generalize inductively.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Vapnik in 'Statistical Learning Theory' (1998) and operationalized for large-scale text by Joachims at ICML 1999, the paper won a 10-year Best Paper Award; Joachims framed the core insight as: there is no reason to learn a global rule when the goal is to classify only a specific, known set of test points.

children.name: 1.4 Reinforcement Learning
children.diff_siblings: Unlike supervised and unsupervised learning, which operate on fixed datasets, Reinforcement Learning formalizes the problem as a Markov Decision Process where an agent learns a policy by receiving scalar reward signals from environment interactions — no labeled examples or static data distribution required.
strengths: Learns sequential decision policies directly from environment feedback, enabling planning over long horizons that single-step prediction models cannot capture
Does not require labeled training data, making it applicable when ground-truth labels are unavailable but a reward signal can be specified (e.g., game score, energy consumption)
Can discover non-obvious strategies that outperform expert human behavior, as demonstrated by AlphaGo surpassing all human Go players by self-play alone
weaknesses: Requires millions of environment interactions before convergence — orders of magnitude more data than supervised learning for equivalent task complexity
Reward function engineering is brittle: sparse, delayed, or misspecified rewards cause the agent to exploit unintended loopholes rather than learning the intended behavior
Policies trained in simulation suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in real environments due to the sim-to-real gap in dynamics and sensor noise
recommended_for: Sequential control problems with a well-defined reward signal and a cheap simulator, such as robotic locomotion or game-playing agents where millions of trials are feasible
Combinatorial optimization tasks (e.g., chip floorplanning, network routing) where the search space is too large for exhaustive methods and each candidate solution can be scored
not_recommended_for: Supervised prediction tasks with abundant labeled data (e.g., image classification, tabular regression), where direct optimization of a loss function converges faster and more reliably
Safety-critical real-world systems where exploratory trial-and-error is unacceptable, such as medical dosing or autonomous driving on public roads without a high-fidelity simulator
children.curiosity: The modern RL framework was consolidated by Chris Watkins in his 1989 PhD thesis 'Learning from Delayed Rewards', which introduced Q-learning and unified the previously separate threads of optimal control, trial-and-error learning, and Sutton's 1988 temporal-difference methods into a single algorithm.

children.name: Model-Free
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Model-Based RL, which explicitly learns a transition function P(s'|s,a) and reward function R(s,a) to plan ahead via simulation, Model-Free RL estimates value functions or policies directly from sampled (s, a, r, s') tuples without ever constructing an internal environment model.
strengths: Avoids model bias: errors in a learned environment model cannot propagate into the policy, since no model is used — the agent optimizes against real transitions only.
Simpler implementation: algorithms such as Q-learning (Watkins, 1989) and SARSA require only a value-table or neural network update per step, with no secondary planning loop.
Scales naturally to high-dimensional, stochastic environments where accurately modeling dynamics is intractable, as seen with DQN on Atari (Mnih et al., 2015).
weaknesses: High sample complexity: learning value functions from scratch via temporal-difference errors requires orders of magnitude more environment interactions than model-based counterparts on the same task.
On-policy variants (SARSA, PPO, A2C) discard off-policy data, so experience from earlier policy iterations cannot be reused, compounding the sample cost.
No explicit world model means the agent cannot reason about hypothetical futures or safely plan in environments where real-world interactions carry physical or financial risk.
recommended_for: Simulated environments with cheap, parallelizable resets — e.g., game engines or physics simulators — where millions of interactions can be collected at low cost and model bias would degrade planning.

Tasks with non-stationary or partially unknown dynamics where building an accurate transition model is unreliable, such as financial trading with regime shifts, and direct policy learning from market data is more robust.
not_recommended_for: Real-world robotics or safety-critical control where each interaction is costly or dangerous and the sample budget is limited to hundreds or low thousands of episodes.

Problems where a compact, accurate dynamics model is already available (e.g., known physics equations), since ignoring it wastes the information and discards the sample-efficiency advantage that model-based planning provides.
children.curiosity: The term 'model-free' was formalized alongside Q-learning in Christopher Watkins's 1989 Cambridge PhD thesis 'Learning from Delayed Rewards', which proved convergence of a direct value-update rule that required no knowledge of transition probabilities — a result later tightened by Watkins and Dayan (1992) in Machine Learning.

children.name: Q-Learning
children.diff_siblings: Unlike SARSA (on-policy) and model-based methods that require a learned environment model, Q-Learning is off-policy and model-free: it updates the Q-table using the greedy max over next-state actions regardless of the policy actually followed, enabling learning from exploratory or arbitrary behavior data.
strengths: Off-policy learning allows reuse of experience from any behavior policy (e.g., human demonstrations or exploratory rollouts) without rerunning the environment.
Converges to the optimal Q-function with probability 1 in finite MDPs, provided all state-action pairs are visited infinitely often and the learning rate satisfies Robbins-Monro conditions.
Simple Bellman update (one scalar per step, no model to maintain) makes it computationally cheap per sample and trivial to implement on tabular problems.
weaknesses: Q-table size grows as |S|×|A|, making pure tabular Q-Learning intractable for continuous or high-dimensional state spaces without function approximation.
Off-policy max operator causes systematic overestimation of Q-values in stochastic environments (addressed by Double Q-Learning, Hasselt 2010), leading to suboptimal policies.
Convergence is slow in practice for large state spaces: sample complexity scales poorly with the number of states, often requiring millions of steps where model-based methods would need far fewer.
recommended_for: Grid-world and discrete navigation tasks (e.g., maze solving, board games with enumerable states) where the full Q-table fits in memory and fast lookup is needed.
Off-policy batch RL settings where logged interaction data from a different (possibly suboptimal) policy must be reused to learn a better policy without additional environment interaction.
not_recommended_for: Environments with continuous or very high-dimensional state/action spaces (e.g., raw pixel inputs, robotic control with many joints) where a flat Q-table is computationally infeasible.
Safety-critical applications requiring conservative behavior near constraint boundaries, since the greedy max update is optimistic and ignores risk, unlike on-policy methods such as SARSA.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Christopher Watkins in his 1989 Cambridge PhD thesis 'Learning from Delayed Rewards'; the formal convergence proof was published by Watkins and Dayan in Machine Learning (1992), establishing Q-Learning as the first provably convergent model-free RL algorithm.
keywords: agent learns by trial and error

children.name: SARSA
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Q-learning, which updates toward the greedy max-Q action regardless of what the agent actually does, SARSA bootstraps from the action genuinely taken at the next step (the full S,A,R,S',A' quintuple), making it an on-policy method that learns the value of the behavior policy rather than the optimal policy.
strengths: Safer exploration: because it accounts for the cost of the exploration policy itself, SARSA avoids cliff-edges and high-risk transitions that Q-learning ignores during training.
Better online performance: in stochastic or risky environments, SARSA accumulates higher cumulative reward during training even when it converges to a slightly sub-optimal policy.

Guaranteed convergence under tabular representation: with decaying epsilon-greedy and sufficient state-action visits, SARSA(0) converges to the optimal Q-function under standard Robbins-Monro conditions.
weaknesses: Slower convergence to the optimal policy than Q-learning because the target includes the exploration noise of the behavior policy, which must decay to zero for optimality.
Policy-coupled learning: the learned Q-values are entangled with the specific epsilon schedule used; changing the exploration strategy invalidates accumulated estimates and requires retraining.
No convergence guarantee with nonlinear function approximation: combining SARSA with neural networks breaks the tabular convergence proof, and instability analogous to the deadly triad can occur.
recommended_for: Safety-critical control tasks with discrete actions where costly exploratory mistakes during training must be minimized, such as robot navigation near obstacles or inventory management with stockout penalties.
Environments with stochastic transitions and rewards where learning a policy that performs well under the actual exploration strategy matters more than finding the theoretical optimum offline.
not_recommended_for: Offline or batch reinforcement learning scenarios, because SARSA requires on-policy data generated by the current behavior policy and cannot efficiently reuse transitions collected under a different policy.
High-dimensional or continuous state-action spaces without function approximation, where the Q-table grows combinatorially and memory and sample complexity become intractable.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rummery and Niranjan (1994) in a Cambridge technical report as 'Modified Connectionist Q-Learning'; the acronym SARSA was coined by Richard Sutton, who noted that the update depends on the full tuple (State, Action, Reward, State, Action), and the name was subsequently adopted universally.

children.name: DQN (Deep Q-Network)
children.diff_siblings: DQN approximates Q-values with a deep convolutional neural network and stabilizes off-policy TD learning through two mechanisms absent in tabular or linear siblings: an experience replay buffer (breaks temporal correlations in the training distribution) and a periodically frozen target network (decouples the moving regression target from the online weights).
strengths: Learns directly from raw high-dimensional inputs (e.g., pixel frames) without hand-crafted feature engineering, via end-to-end gradient descent through conv layers.
Off-policy training with experience replay reuses past transitions multiple times, achieving high sample efficiency relative to purely on-policy model-free methods.

A single network learns policies for qualitatively different tasks (e.g., 49 Atari games) using the same architecture and hyperparameters, demonstrating broad generalization across discrete-action domains.
weaknesses: The max operator in the Bellman target causes systematic overestimation of Q-values, leading to propagating value errors and suboptimal policies in environments with many similar actions.
Restricted to finite discrete action spaces; applying DQN to continuous control requires discretization, which grows exponentially with action dimensionality.
Convergence is fragile: performance is highly sensitive to the target network update frequency, replay buffer size, and learning rate — small misconfigurations cause divergence.
recommended_for: High-dimensional discrete-action control tasks where the observation is a raw image sequence (e.g., video game emulators, UI navigation), because the conv architecture extracts spatial features and replay removes frame-to-frame correlation.
Offline or data-efficient settings where the same environment transitions must be reused across many gradient updates, since the replay buffer decouples data collection from optimization.
not_recommended_for: Continuous or high-cardinality action spaces (e.g., robotic joint torques, recommendation with millions of items), where the argmax over Q-values is intractable without coarse discretization.

Safety-critical or on-policy settings where the agent must account for exploration risk, since DQN's greedy policy ignores the cost of exploratory actions that SARSA-style on-policy methods naturally penalize.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Mnih et al. at DeepMind (2013, refined in Nature 2015), DQN was the first algorithm to train a single agent to superhuman level on 29 of 49 Atari 2600 games from raw pixels — a result that launched the modern deep reinforcement learning era.

children.name: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike TRPO, which enforces a KL-divergence constraint via expensive second-order optimization, PPO approximates the same trust region by clipping the probability ratio r_t(θ) to [1−ε, 1+ε] in a first-order surrogate objective, achieving comparable stability at a fraction of the computational cost.
strengths: Clip-based trust region eliminates costly Hessian computation, making each update O(n) rather than O(n²) compared to TRPO.
On-policy actor-critic design allows stable credit assignment across long horizons using Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), reducing variance without introducing off-policy bias.
Single ε hyperparameter (typically 0.1–0.2) controls policy update magnitude, making tuning far simpler than the constraint radius in TRPO or the learning-rate sensitivity of vanilla policy gradient.
weaknesses: Strictly on-policy: collected rollouts are discarded after each update, requiring fresh environment interactions every iteration and making it 3–10× less sample-efficient than off-policy methods like SAC.
Coordinating four models simultaneously in RLHF settings (actor, critic, reward model, reference model) multiplies GPU memory requirements and complicates distributed training at scale.
Performance degrades sharply with sparse or delayed rewards because the advantage estimator collapses toward zero, effectively stopping learning until a reward signal is received.
recommended_for: Continuous control tasks (MuJoCo locomotion, robotic manipulation) where stable, incremental policy updates are critical and environment resets are cheap enough to afford on-policy sampling.
RLHF fine-tuning of language models where the action space is a fixed vocabulary and a pre-trained reward model provides dense turn-level feedback (e.g., InstructGPT-style alignment pipelines).
not_recommended_for: Environments with extremely sparse rewards and expensive simulation (e.g., molecular docking, long-horizon physical assembly), where off-policy replay and model-based planning are needed to amortize sample cost.
Stationary tabular MDPs with small, discrete action spaces where Q-learning variants converge orders of magnitude faster without the overhead of maintaining a separate value network.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Schulman et al. at OpenAI (arXiv 2017), PPO became the default training algorithm for OpenAI Five (Dota 2) in 2018, running on 256 GPUs and 128,000 CPU cores simultaneously — the largest single-game RL training run at that time.

children.name: SAC (Soft Actor-Critic)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike deterministic off-policy siblings (DDPG, TD3) or clipped-surrogate on-policy ones (PPO), SAC optimizes a maximum-entropy objective that simultaneously maximizes expected return and policy entropy, producing a stochastic actor that explores intrinsically without separate noise injection.
strengths: Off-policy replay buffer reuse gives 3-5x better sample efficiency than PPO on MuJoCo benchmarks, reaching the same asymptotic performance with far fewer environment steps.
Automatic temperature (α) tuning via a dual optimization treats entropy as a constraint, removing the most critical hyperparameter and making SAC robust across tasks without per-environment tuning.
Stochastic policy with entropy bonus naturally avoids premature convergence to local optima in multi-modal reward landscapes where deterministic policies (TD3) often get trapped.
weaknesses: Two separate Q-networks plus actor and temperature networks increase memory and forward-pass cost compared to single-critic algorithms, making it heavier to deploy on memory-constrained hardware.

Originally designed for continuous action spaces; adapting to discrete actions (Christodoulou 2019) requires reparameterizing the policy as Categorical and setting a task-specific target entropy heuristic.
In sparse-reward or highly stochastic environments, the entropy bonus can delay exploitation too long, causing slower convergence than on-policy methods like PPO that use fresh trajectory data.
recommended_for: Continuous-control robotics tasks (locomotion, dexterous manipulation) where simulator calls are expensive and sample efficiency matters more than wall-clock training time.
Environments with multi-modal optimal policies (e.g., maze navigation, contact-rich manipulation) where the entropy term prevents the policy from collapsing to a single suboptimal mode.
not_recommended_for: Discrete action games (Atari) where the categorical action space and high stochasticity of game frames make value-based methods (Rainbow DQN) more stable and better tuned.
Real-time safety-critical control with strict determinism requirements, where a stochastic policy that samples different actions in the same state is unacceptable.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Haarnoja et al. (2018) in 'Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor' (ICML 2018), SAC's maximum-entropy formulation traces back to Ziebart et al.'s 2008 maximum causal entropy framework for inverse RL, repurposed here as an exploration and robustness mechanism.

children.name: A3C/A2C
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DQN (which uses an experience replay buffer and a value-only target) or pure policy gradient methods, A3C/A2C trains an actor (policy) and a critic (state-value function) jointly, using the advantage function A(s,a)=R-V(s) to reduce gradient variance, and stabilizes learning through multiple parallel environment copies instead of replay memory.
strengths: Eliminates the experience replay buffer by using parallel actors to decorrelate training samples, reducing memory overhead to O(n_workers) rather than O(replay_buffer_size)
The advantage estimate A(s,a)=R_t - V(s_t) directly reduces policy gradient variance compared to REINFORCE, enabling faster convergence on sparse-reward tasks
A2C's synchronous batched updates are GPU-efficient: all workers finish a rollout segment before a single large gradient step, saturating GPU throughput unlike asynchronous variants
weaknesses: On-policy: collected rollouts are discarded after each update, making sample efficiency far lower than off-policy methods like SAC or DQN for environments where interaction is costly
No trust-region constraint on policy updates — a poorly tuned learning rate can cause catastrophic policy collapse, a problem PPO specifically addresses with its clipped surrogate objective
A3C's asynchronous gradient accumulation introduces stale gradients (workers read parameters that are already outdated), producing noisy updates and non-smooth convergence curves
recommended_for: Discrete-action game environments (e.g., Atari) where environment steps are cheap and many parallel CPU workers can be used, exploiting A3C's asynchronous multi-core design
Continuous control tasks with moderate horizon length where a shared CNN/RNN backbone must encode both policy and value simultaneously, benefiting from A2C's GPU-batched synchronous rollouts
not_recommended_for: Real-world robotics or expensive simulators where each environment step has significant cost, as on-policy rollout discard makes sample efficiency prohibitive compared to SAC or TD3

Problems requiring very fine-grained policy stability guarantees, where PPO's clipped objective or TRPO's KL constraint are needed to prevent the large, destabilizing policy updates A2C/A3C can produce
children.curiosity: Introduced by Mnih et al. at DeepMind (ICML 2016, arXiv:1602.01783), A3C was the first deep RL algorithm to achieve strong Atari performance without experience replay, running 16 parallel CPU threads on a single machine and matching or surpassing DQN's score in half the wall-clock training time.

children.name: TRPO (Trust Region Policy Optimization)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike vanilla policy gradient methods (REINFORCE) that take unconstrained gradient steps and PPO that uses a clipped surrogate objective, TRPO enforces a hard KL-divergence constraint between old and new policies, solved via conjugate gradient and a backtracking line search on the Fisher information matrix.
strengths: Monotonic policy improvement guarantee per iteration — the KL trust region constraint prevents catastrophic policy collapse that unclipped gradient steps cause.
Effective on continuous control tasks with high-dimensional action spaces (e.g., MuJoCo locomotion) where unconstrained updates destabilize training.
Requires minimal hyperparameter tuning compared to vanilla policy gradients because the constraint radius delta implicitly governs step size.
weaknesses: Conjugate gradient + Fisher-vector products make each update O(kd) with k CG iterations, adding substantial per-step overhead versus first-order methods like PPO.
Fisher information matrix is often ill-conditioned, so the conjugate gradient solution is inaccurate with the small iteration budget TRPO uses in practice.
Poor performance on pixel-based discrete-action environments (e.g., Atari), where value-based methods like DQN outperform it empirically.
recommended_for: Continuous-action robotic control (joint torques, locomotion) where policy collapse is costly and stable monotonic improvement is required.
Research settings where theoretical guarantees of improvement matter more than wall-clock speed, and the policy network has tens of thousands of parameters.
not_recommended_for: Large-scale training with neural networks of millions of parameters, where the conjugate gradient and Hessian-vector products per update become prohibitively expensive.
Discrete, pixel-based environments (Atari-style) where the second-order overhead yields no empirical advantage over simpler value-based or clipped-objective methods.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Schulman, Levine, Abbeel, Jordan, and Moritz (ICML 2015, arXiv 1502.05477), TRPO was the first deep RL algorithm to provide a formal monotonic improvement theorem for stochastic policies, deriving the trust region bound from Kakade and Langford's (2002) conservative policy iteration theory.

children.name: TD3 (Twin Delayed DDPG)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DDPG (single critic, prone to Q-overestimation) or SAC (stochastic entropy-maximizing policy), TD3 uses two independent critic networks whose minimum is used for target computation, a delayed actor update schedule, and Gaussian noise injected into target actions during critic training — three architectural fixes that jointly suppress overestimation bias and stabilize learning.
strengths: Twin critics with min-operator provably reduce Q-value overestimation bias that destabilizes DDPG, yielding more reliable policy gradients
Delayed actor updates (actor updated every 2 critic steps) let the value function converge enough before each policy gradient step, reducing compounding errors
Target policy smoothing (noise on target actions during Bellman backup) prevents the actor from exploiting narrow Q-function spikes, improving generalization across similar states
weaknesses: Deterministic policy requires explicit external noise (e.g., Ornstein-Uhlenbeck or Gaussian) for exploration, making exploration less principled than SAC's built-in entropy term
Hyperparameter sensitivity is high: policy update delay, target noise std, and noise clip interact, and poor choices cause the actor to lag or diverge
Restricted to continuous action spaces; cannot be applied to discrete-action problems without architectural modifications
recommended_for: Continuous robotic control tasks (e.g., MuJoCo locomotion: HalfCheetah, Ant) where deterministic precision is valued over maximum exploration and sample counts are in the millions
Industrial continuous-control simulators where a well-tuned, reproducible policy is needed and the environment reward is dense enough for off-policy learning
not_recommended_for: Environments with sparse rewards or requiring extensive exploration, where SAC's entropy maximization yields far better coverage of the state space
Discrete or mixed action spaces (e.g., Atari, combinatorial scheduling) where the deterministic continuous-action architecture does not apply directly
children.curiosity: Introduced by Scott Fujimoto, Herke van Hoof, and David Meger (ICML 2018) in 'Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods'; the twin-critic idea was directly inspired by Double Q-learning (van Hasselt et al., 2016), but applied to the actor-critic setting where overestimation had been observed to be even more severe than in tabular methods.

children.name: Rainbow DQN
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DQN variants that extend a single axis (e.g., Double DQN fixes overestimation, Dueling DQN separates state-value from advantage), Rainbow simultaneously integrates six orthogonal improvements — double Q-learning, prioritized replay, dueling architecture, multi-step returns, distributional Q (C51), and noisy nets — into a single agent.
strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art sample efficiency on Atari 2600: the ablation in Hessel et al. (2018) shows the combined agent reaches human-level performance with roughly 7x fewer environment steps than any single-component variant.

Distributional head (C51) models the full return distribution rather than a scalar expectation, making the agent robust to reward variance and multi-modal return landscapes where a mean estimate is misleading.

Noisy nets replace epsilon-greedy exploration with learned, state-dependent noise in the linear layers, enabling richer exploration strategies that adapt as training progresses without requiring a separate exploration schedule.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter surface multiplies across all six components (e.g., priority exponent alpha, n-step horizon, number of C51 atoms), making tuning substantially harder than tuning any individual DQN variant.

Computational and memory cost is significantly higher than base DQN: prioritized replay requires a sum-tree data structure, the distributional head multiplies the output layer by the number of atoms (e.g., 51), and noisy layers add trainable noise parameters.
Restricted to discrete action spaces inherited from DQN; direct application to continuous control (e.g., robotics, locomotion) is not possible without architectural replacement of the Q-head.
recommended_for: Atari-style discrete-action game benchmarks where sample efficiency matters and a large replay buffer (1M transitions) is feasible, because Rainbow's prioritized multi-step distributional learning extracts maximum signal per stored transition.

Research baselines requiring a strong model-free off-policy reference point in discrete action domains, since Rainbow's ablation framework makes it straightforward to isolate the contribution of individual components.
not_recommended_for: Continuous action spaces (e.g., MuJoCo locomotion, robotic manipulation), where actor-critic methods such as SAC or TD3 are architecturally appropriate and Rainbow's Q-head cannot be applied directly.

Resource-constrained or real-time deployment settings where inference latency and memory are limited, because the dueling-distributional network with noisy layers and a large prioritized replay buffer imposes non-trivial overhead compared to simpler DQN variants.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hessel et al. at DeepMind (AAAI 2018, arXiv 1710.02298), Rainbow's ablation study revealed that the three components most critical to its gains are distributional RL, multi-step returns, and prioritized replay — while double Q-learning and the dueling architecture provided only marginal incremental improvement within the combined agent.

children.name: HER (Hindsight Experience Replay)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other model-free algorithms (DQN, DDPG, PPO, SAC) that learn directly from reward signals, HER is a replay buffer augmentation strategy: it retroactively relabels failed transitions with the goal actually achieved, converting zero-reward episodes into informative training data without changing the underlying policy optimization.
strengths: Solves binary sparse-reward tasks (0/-1) that cause DDPG and DQN to fail entirely, by synthetically generating successful experiences from every failed trajectory
Algorithm-agnostic wrapper compatible with any off-policy method (DQN, DDPG, TD3, SAC) requiring no changes to the policy gradient or Q-update equations
Produces an implicit curriculum: early relabeled goals are trivially reachable, and as the policy improves the reachable set expands toward the true target
weaknesses: Restricted to goal-conditioned policies where state and goal share the same representation space; cannot be applied to tasks without an explicit goal embedding
Relabeling strategy (e.g., 'future', 'episode', 'random') must be tuned per task — wrong choice inflates replay bias and slows convergence
Introduces distributional shift: transitions relabeled with a hindsight goal are off-policy with respect to the original goal, which can destabilize Q-value estimates in long-horizon tasks
recommended_for: Robotic manipulation with binary success/failure feedback (e.g., peg-in-hole, pick-and-place) where the achieved end-effector position can serve directly as a hindsight goal
Multi-goal navigation in discrete or continuous state spaces where goals are positions and reward is 0 only at exact target — dense reward shaping is unavailable or undesirable
not_recommended_for: Tasks with dense, shaped reward signals where every step already provides informative gradient; HER's relabeling adds overhead with no benefit in that regime
Non-goal-conditioned tasks (e.g., game-playing, locomotion without a target) where there is no natural 'achieved goal' to relabel transitions with
children.curiosity: Introduced by Andrychowicz et al. at OpenAI (NeurIPS 2017) after observing that humans learn from failure by imagining alternative objectives — the paper showed that DDPG alone solved 0 of 3 robotic tasks while DDPG+HER solved all 3 nearly perfectly, despite the reward being identically sparse in both cases.

children.name: IMPALA (Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architecture)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike A3C (which broadcasts gradients to a shared parameter server) or synchronous PPO (which requires all workers to finish before each update), IMPALA fully decouples actors from the learner: actors stream raw trajectories to a central GPU learner at high throughput, and the resulting policy lag is corrected by V-trace, a clipped importance-sampling return estimator.
strengths: Throughput scales nearly linearly with the number of actors (hundreds to thousands) because actors never block waiting for gradient synchronization.
V-trace bounds the variance of off-policy corrections by clipping importance-sampling ratios at c and rho, preventing the instability that plagues fully off-policy methods under large policy lag.
A single GPU learner processes mini-batches continuously, achieving >30x the data throughput of single-machine A3C while maintaining comparable data efficiency.
weaknesses: V-trace is designed for mild off-policy drift; when actors lag many updates behind the learner the clipped ratios introduce bias, making IMPALA poorly suited to strongly off-policy replay settings.
The centralized learner is a single point of failure and a communication bottleneck: network bandwidth between actors and learner limits scaling on commodity hardware.

Requires careful tuning of the unroll length and the clipping thresholds (c, rho) in V-trace; wrong values cause either high bias (too much clipping) or high variance (too little clipping) in the return estimates.
recommended_for: Large-scale multi-task RL on dozens of discrete-action environments simultaneously (e.g., training a single agent across 57 Atari games), where the decoupled actor pool naturally parallelizes environment interaction.
Environments with fast simulation but expensive policy inference (e.g., complex 3-D physics), where offloading inference to CPU actors frees the GPU learner to maximize gradient throughput.
not_recommended_for: Single-environment, sample-constrained settings (e.g., real-robot learning with limited resets) where the overhead of distributed infrastructure yields no throughput benefit and PPO's on-policy guarantees are preferable.

Problems requiring very long-horizon credit assignment without abundant compute, since V-trace clipping shortens the effective return horizon and can underestimate values for rewards that arrive many steps after the action.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Espeholt et al. (DeepMind, ICML 2018), IMPALA was the first distributed RL system to demonstrate that a single architecture could reach human-level performance across all 57 Atari games simultaneously, a feat no prior single-task agent had achieved at that scale.

children.name: Model-Based
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Model-Free methods that learn value functions or policies directly from environment interactions, Model-Based RL explicitly learns a transition dynamics model T(s'|s,a) and reward model R(s,a), then uses that world model to plan or generate synthetic rollouts without additional real-environment samples.
strengths: Sample efficiency: by reusing a learned dynamics model to generate synthetic transitions (as in Dyna-Q, Sutton 1990), the agent can improve its policy with orders of magnitude fewer real environment interactions than model-free counterparts
Enables lookahead planning (e.g., MCTS, MPC) so the agent can evaluate action sequences over a finite horizon before committing, which is critical when real interactions are expensive or irreversible
Learned model is interpretable and transferable — the dynamics model can be reused across tasks with the same physics, or queried to detect out-of-distribution states before acting
weaknesses: Model error compounds over multi-step rollouts: small per-step prediction errors accumulate exponentially, causing the agent to optimize against an increasingly inaccurate model and often degrading final policy quality

Learning an accurate dynamics model in high-dimensional or discontinuous state spaces (e.g., contact-rich manipulation) requires large neural network ensembles and extensive real data, narrowing the sample-efficiency advantage
Planning overhead is significant: methods like PETS run at ~1 Hz even on GPU, making real-time control in fast physical systems impractical without major approximation
recommended_for: Low-data robotic manipulation or locomotion tasks (e.g., MuJoCo Hopper/HalfCheetah) where real rollouts are costly and a compact Gaussian dynamics model can be learned within a few hundred episodes

Simulation-to-real transfer pipelines where the learned dynamics model can be pre-trained in a cheap simulator and then fine-tuned on a small number of real interactions, using the model's uncertainty estimates to stay within the reliable region
not_recommended_for: High-frequency control loops (> 100 Hz) with hard real-time constraints, where the planning computation of MCTS or ensemble MPC exceeds the available time budget per step

Discrete combinatorial environments with very large branching factors (e.g., full-board Go without heavy GPU resources), where the state-space is too vast for the learned transition model to cover reliably without massive compute
children.curiosity: The foundational Model-Based RL framework, Dyna, was introduced by Richard Sutton in 1990 ('Integrated Architectures for Learning, Planning, and Reacting Based on Approximating Dynamic Programming', ICML 1990); it showed that interleaving real experience with simulated model-generated transitions allows a tabular agent to converge to the optimal policy with a fraction of the real interactions needed by pure model-free Q-learning.

children.name: Dyna-Q
children.diff_siblings: Dyna-Q interleaves real environment steps with tabular one-step Q-planning on a deterministic lookup-table world model, uniquely coupling model learning and value updating in a single online loop rather than separating planning into a distinct offline phase.
strengths: Reaches near-optimal policy with far fewer real environment interactions than model-free Q-learning — Sutton's maze benchmarks show convergence in ~200 trials vs. 1000+ for plain Q-learning.
The world model is built incrementally from each transition at zero extra cost, so no offline data collection phase is required before planning begins.
Number of planning steps per real step (n) is a single hyperparameter that linearly trades computation for sample efficiency, making the algorithm easy to tune.
weaknesses: The tabular model stores one deterministic (s, a) → (s', r) entry per pair, so stochastic environments cause the model to memorize only the last-observed outcome, corrupting planning.
Memory and compute scale with the number of unique (state, action) pairs, making the approach intractable for continuous or high-dimensional state spaces without function approximation.
Planning samples past (state, action) pairs uniformly at random, ignoring which simulated transitions would reduce value-function error the most — a problem addressed by Prioritized Sweeping.
recommended_for: Small discrete environments (grid worlds, simple games) where the full (s, a) table fits in memory and rapid sample efficiency is needed, such as robotics simulators with cheap resets.

Scenarios where real environment interactions are expensive but compute is cheap, and the dynamics are approximately deterministic — e.g., operational-research scheduling tasks with known transition logic.
not_recommended_for: Continuous state or action spaces (e.g., robotic locomotion, Atari pixels) where a flat lookup table cannot represent the model without exponential memory growth.
Stochastic environments with multi-modal transition distributions (e.g., traffic flow, financial markets), where the deterministic last-observation model introduces systematic planning errors.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Richard Sutton in 'Dyna, an Integrated Architecture for Learning, Planning, and Reacting' (ACM SIGART Bulletin, 1991), Dyna-Q was among the first algorithms to formally unify model-free TD learning and model-based planning into a single agent loop, directly influencing the field's distinction between the two paradigms.

children.name: World Models
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other model-based RL approaches that learn explicit transition functions in observation space (Dyna) or probabilistic ensembles (MBPO), World Models compress raw observations into a low-dimensional latent code via a VAE and model dynamics entirely within that latent space using a mixture-density RNN, enabling the agent to be trained inside a generated 'dream' rollout rather than the real environment.
strengths: Decouples representation learning (VAE) from dynamics modeling (MDN-RNN) and control (CMA-ES controller), so each component can be optimized independently with far fewer parameters in the controller (~1,000 weights).
Supports 'dream training': the controller can be evolved entirely inside simulated latent rollouts, reducing costly environment interactions to only what is needed for world-model training.
Latent-space rollouts are orders of magnitude faster than pixel-space simulation, enabling thousands of imagined episodes per wall-clock second on a single GPU.
weaknesses: Prediction errors compound autoregressively across long dream horizons, causing the learned policy to exploit model inaccuracies and degrade when transferred back to the real environment.
The VAE bottleneck discards information not useful for reconstruction, potentially losing task-relevant details (e.g., small but critical objects), which the dynamics model never sees.
The mixture-density RNN struggles to capture sharply multimodal or contact-rich transitions, causing the world model to underfit environments with abrupt, discontinuous dynamics.
recommended_for: Visually rich environments with pixel-based observations (e.g., racing games, 3D navigation) where raw-pixel planning is too expensive but a compact latent representation is sufficient for control.
Settings with a tight interaction budget — simulation-constrained robotics or game AI — where training the policy inside dreams drastically reduces the number of real environment steps required.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring precise physical contact or discontinuous dynamics (e.g., dexterous manipulation), where the smooth Gaussian/MDN latent transitions systematically misrepresent reality.

Environments with non-stationary or rapidly shifting dynamics (e.g., opponent adaptation in competitive games), where a fixed world model trained offline quickly becomes stale and misleads the policy.
children.curiosity: Introduced by David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber (2018) in 'World Models' (arXiv:1803.10122), the paper demonstrated that a controller trained exclusively inside the agent's own dream — never seeing the real environment during policy search — could still solve VizDoom's TakeCover task, scoring 1,092 ± 556 compared to 820 for human players.
keywords: learning a simulator of the environment
training agents inside a learned model

children.name: Multi-Agent
children.diff_siblings: Unlike single-agent RL variants (model-free, model-based, policy gradient), Multi-Agent RL replaces the single MDP with a Markov game where N agents act simultaneously, making the environment non-stationary from each agent's perspective and coupling rewards and state transitions across all agents' joint actions.
strengths: Models emergent coordination and competition: agents develop strategies (cooperation, negotiation, deception) that cannot arise in a single-agent MDP, enabling solutions to decentralized problems with interdependent decisions.

Parallelism in execution: at inference time each agent acts independently with its local policy, making decentralized deployment scalable to large systems (e.g., hundreds of traffic signals) without a central controller.

Covers the full game-theoretic spectrum (fully cooperative to zero-sum) within one framework, allowing the same MARL infrastructure to train QMIX for cooperative tasks and minimax Q-learning for adversarial ones.
weaknesses: Non-stationarity breaks convergence guarantees: because all agents learn concurrently, each agent's environment is a non-MDP from its own perspective, invalidating standard single-agent convergence proofs and making training unstable.

Joint action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, making centralized value-function methods (e.g., centralized Q over joint actions) computationally intractable beyond a handful of agents without factorization tricks like VDN or QMIX.

Reward credit assignment is hard in cooperative settings: when a shared global reward is the only signal, determining each individual agent's contribution (the multi-agent credit assignment problem) requires additional mechanisms that add architectural complexity.
recommended_for: Decentralized control of physically interacting systems with local sensors — e.g., fleets of autonomous vehicles at an intersection, where each vehicle observes only nearby traffic but collective behavior determines safety and throughput.

Competitive or mixed-motive game environments with discrete turns or simultaneous moves — e.g., multi-player strategy games or auction mechanisms where each participant's optimal policy depends explicitly on the evolving strategies of opponents.
not_recommended_for: Problems with a single decision-maker and a stationary environment: standard single-agent RL or even supervised learning will converge faster and with stronger theoretical guarantees than MARL, which adds unnecessary non-stationarity overhead.

Settings where the number of interacting entities is very large (thousands+) and their interactions are homogeneous: mean-field approximations or classical operations-research methods (e.g., linear programming for traffic assignment) are more tractable than explicit multi-agent joint modeling.
children.curiosity: The formal MARL framework was established by Michael Littman (1994) in 'Markov Games as a Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning' (ICML 1994), which introduced minimax Q-learning for two-player zero-sum games — the first algorithm to extend Watkins' Q-learning to a game-theoretic setting with convergence proof under a Nash equilibrium objective.

children.name: MADDPG
children.diff_siblings: Unlike QMIX (value decomposition, cooperative-only, discrete actions) and COMA (single shared critic, counterfactual advantage), MADDPG assigns each agent its own centralized critic that observes all agents' actions and states, while keeping actors decentralized and operating on local observations, enabling continuous action spaces in cooperative, competitive, and mixed settings simultaneously.
strengths: Works natively with continuous action spaces via deterministic policy gradient, whereas value-decomposition siblings (QMIX, VDN) require discrete actions or workarounds
Per-agent centralized critics see the full joint action space during training, stabilizing learning against the non-stationarity caused by simultaneously adapting agents
Applicable to cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive environments with no architectural change, since each agent's critic models opponents' behavior independently
weaknesses: Critic input size grows linearly with agent count (each critic receives all N agents' observations and actions), making training cost prohibitive beyond roughly 10-20 agents
Inherits DDPG's sensitivity to hyperparameters and replay buffer size; off-policy training with deterministic policies can diverge in highly stochastic or non-stationary environments
Assumes full observability of other agents' actions at training time, which is impractical when opponents' action spaces are unknown or partially observable
recommended_for: Robotics swarms or multi-vehicle control with continuous joint torques/velocities where discrete-action methods cannot represent the action space faithfully
Mixed cooperative-competitive games (e.g., predator-prey, multi-team sports simulation) where a single shared critic cannot correctly assign credit across opposing teams
not_recommended_for: Environments with dozens to hundreds of agents, where the O(N) critic input growth makes per-agent networks computationally intractable compared to factored methods like QMIX
Purely cooperative tasks with discrete actions and tight communication constraints, where QMIX or MAPPO achieve equivalent or better performance with lower memory and compute cost
children.curiosity: Introduced by Lowe et al. (OpenAI, 2017) in 'Multi-Agent Actor-Critic for Mixed Cooperative-Competitive Environments' (NeurIPS 2017); the authors also released the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) benchmark alongside the paper, which became the de facto standard testbed for continuous-action MARL research for several years.

children.name: QMIX
children.diff_siblings: Unlike VDN (which sums per-agent Q-values linearly) and MADDPG/COMA (which use centralized critics without structural decomposition), QMIX enforces a monotonicity constraint via a hypernetwork-generated mixing network whose weights are non-negative, ensuring that the joint Q-value is a monotonic function of each agent's individual Q-value — preserving the IGM property without assuming linearity.
strengths: Scalable cooperative training: the mixing network complexity grows linearly with agent count, making it tractable for dozens of agents where fully centralized Q-tables are exponential.

Allows rich non-linear factorization: by conditioning mixing-network weights on the global state via hypernetworks, it can represent strictly larger classes of joint Q-functions than VDN's additive decomposition.
CTDE (Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution): each agent acts using only its local observation at execution time, requiring no inter-agent communication at runtime.
weaknesses: Monotonicity constraint is sufficient but not necessary for IGM, so QMIX cannot represent joint Q-functions where a globally optimal joint action requires one agent's local Q-value to decrease — it fails on non-monotonic payoff matrices.
Poorly handles competitive or mixed-motive settings: the architecture assumes full cooperativity and a shared reward; applying it to heterogeneous-reward scenarios yields undefined behavior.

Hypernetwork conditioning on the global state is unavailable at execution time — any state information used during training cannot assist decentralized decision-making, creating a train/test information gap.
recommended_for: Cooperative multi-robot or multi-drone tasks (e.g., StarCraft II micromanagement) where agents share a single team reward and must coordinate without runtime communication.
Decentralized sensor networks or warehouse robotics where each unit has only local partial observations but a centralized simulator is available during training to supply global state to the mixer.
not_recommended_for: Games or problems with non-monotonic payoff structures (e.g., coordination tasks with 'miscoordination penalties') where the optimal joint Q-function cannot be expressed as a monotonic combination of individual utilities.
Mixed cooperative-competitive environments (e.g., general-sum games) where agents have individual reward signals that conflict, as QMIX's architecture presupposes a single shared team reward.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rashid et al. (ICML 2018) and later extended in JMLR (2020), QMIX was the first method to prove that enforcing non-negative mixing-network weights is sufficient to guarantee the IGM property, enabling tractable greedy action selection in joint action spaces that would otherwise be exponential in the number of agents.

children.name: MAPPO (Multi-Agent PPO)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike value-decomposition siblings (QMIX, VDN) that factorize a joint Q-function, and unlike off-policy siblings (MADDPG), MAPPO uses a shared centralized critic with global state access under the on-policy PPO clipped-surrogate objective, giving each agent's actor a trust-region update grounded in joint observations without ever storing a replay buffer.
strengths: Centralized critic conditioned on global state provides accurate credit assignment in partial-observability settings where each agent sees only a local observation
On-policy clipped surrogate objective (epsilon=0.2) prevents destructive policy updates without requiring a replay buffer, making training stable across heterogeneous agent populations
Empirically matches or exceeds off-policy baselines (QMIX, MADDPG) on SMAC benchmarks with identical hyperparameters across tasks, as shown by Yu et al. (2022)
weaknesses: On-policy data collection discards all experience after each update, requiring far more environment interactions than off-policy methods when the environment is slow or expensive to simulate
Centralized critic requires access to the global state at training time, which is unavailable in fully decentralized real-world deployments where agents cannot share raw observations
Shared global reward broadcast to all agents does not distinguish individual contributions, causing credit-assignment ambiguity in teams where agents have asymmetric roles
recommended_for: Cooperative tasks with a simulator that can be parallelized cheaply (e.g., StarCraft micromanagement, multi-robot navigation in MuJoCo) where the global state is observable during training
Research baselines for cooperative MARL: the algorithm's minimal hyperparameter sensitivity and open-source implementation make it the standard reference point when comparing new CTDE methods
not_recommended_for: Real-world multi-robot systems where training interactions are costly and sample efficiency is critical, as on-policy rollouts cannot reuse past experience
Competitive or mixed-cooperative-competitive settings, since MAPPO's centralized critic and shared reward formulation assume a fully cooperative team objective
children.curiosity: Introduced by Chao Yu, Akash Velu, Eugene Vinitsky et al. (NeurIPS 2022) under the title 'The Surprising Effectiveness of PPO in Cooperative Multi-Agent Games'; the paper showed that five implementation details (value normalization, input representation, data reuse epochs, PPO clipping, and death masking) were sufficient for vanilla PPO to match or outperform specialized off-policy MARL algorithms that had been the field's standard for years.

children.name: 1.5 Causal / Heterogeneous Inference
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other ML subcategories that minimize predictive loss on outcomes, causal/heterogeneous inference methods target the estimation of individual or conditional average treatment effects (CATE) by explicitly modeling the counterfactual gap between treated and untreated potential outcomes.
strengths: Produces valid confidence intervals for treatment effects even when high-dimensional nuisance functions (propensity score, outcome model) are fit by ML — achieved via Neyman-orthogonal scores and cross-fitting (Double ML, Chernozhukov et al. 2018)
Meta-learner decomposition (S/T/X/DR-learner) allows any off-the-shelf ML model to be repurposed for CATE estimation without rewriting the base algorithm
Causal forests provide honest, asymptotically normal point estimates of heterogeneous effects at the individual level, enabling statistically rigorous subgroup discovery
weaknesses: All methods assume unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounders) — an untestable assumption that, if violated, produces biased CATE estimates regardless of model sophistication
Positivity violations (subgroups where one treatment arm is nearly absent) cause extreme propensity weights and high-variance estimates, collapsing the effective sample size for those subgroups

CATE evaluation is fundamentally hard: the true individual treatment effect is never observed, so standard cross-validation on held-out outcomes does not measure causal accuracy — specialized proxies (R-loss, plug-in DR) are needed
recommended_for: Randomized experiments or quasi-experiments (observational studies with rich covariate adjustment) where the goal is to find which patient or customer subgroups benefit most from a treatment — e.g., personalized medicine RCT data with hundreds of baseline covariates

Policy evaluation pipelines where both the average effect and its heterogeneity across subgroups must be reported with confidence intervals, such as labor-market program evaluation using administrative records
not_recommended_for: Pure prediction tasks where the causal direction is irrelevant — using a CATE estimator to forecast an outcome wastes the orthogonalization overhead and yields no benefit over standard supervised learning

Settings where treatment assignment is fully deterministic for large subgroups (zero propensity overlap), since positivity is violated and no causal estimator can recover unbiased effects without strong extrapolation assumptions
children.curiosity: The foundational guarantee for this field was established by Chernozhukov et al. (2018) in 'Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Structural Parameters' (The Econometrics Journal), proving that cross-fitted Neyman-orthogonal estimators achieve root-n convergence and valid inference even when the nuisance models converge at slower ML rates.

children.name: Causal Forest
children.diff_siblings: Unlike meta-learners (S/T/X-learner) that plug any base estimator into a multi-step recipe, Causal Forest builds trees that split directly on treatment-effect heterogeneity using Neyman-orthogonal scores and honest sample splitting, producing asymptotically normal, pointwise confidence intervals without a separate CATE modeling stage.
strengths: Honest splitting (separate subsamples for tree structure and leaf estimation) eliminates in-sample overfitting bias, enabling valid confidence intervals for each individual CATE estimate.
Double-robustness via residualization of both outcome and treatment on covariates before splitting makes estimates consistent even if one nuisance model is misspecified.

Variable importance is derived directly from splitting frequency on treatment-effect gradients, yielding interpretable covariate rankings tied causally to effect heterogeneity rather than to outcome prediction.
weaknesses: Honest splitting halves the effective sample for both structure search and estimation, requiring roughly 4x more observations than a standard random forest to achieve comparable precision.
Assumes unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounders); unlike IV-based siblings, it has no identification strategy for settings with endogenous treatment selection.

Confidence intervals are pointwise and asymptotic; simultaneous inference over many subgroups requires additional corrections (e.g., Bonferroni or bootstrap), which are not built into the standard grf implementation.
recommended_for: Randomized experiments or observational studies with a rich covariate set (50-500 features) where the goal is to rank subgroups by treatment response for policy targeting (e.g., which patients benefit most from a drug).
Policy evaluation datasets with 5,000+ observations where heterogeneous treatment effects must come with valid uncertainty quantification rather than just point estimates.
not_recommended_for: Small samples (n < 500): honest splitting leaves too few observations per leaf for reliable CATE estimation and valid coverage of the confidence intervals.

Settings with strong unmeasured confounding where treatment assignment cannot be plausibly treated as ignorable given observed covariates, as the orthogonalization step does not correct for latent selection.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Wager and Athey (2018) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, the paper proved that individual tree predictions are asymptotically Gaussian and unbiased under honesty — the first formal statistical inference guarantee for a forest-based CATE estimator.

children.name: Double ML (DML)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike meta-learners (T/S/X-Learner) that directly fit conditional outcome models, and unlike Causal Forests that estimate heterogeneous effects non-parametrically, DML targets a single low-dimensional causal parameter by residualizing both outcome and treatment on covariates via Neyman-orthogonal moment conditions and K-fold cross-fitting, which removes first-order regularization bias from the ML nuisance estimators.
strengths: Valid frequentist confidence intervals for the ATE/LATE even when nuisance functions (outcome and propensity) are estimated with high-dimensional ML — asymptotic normality holds under root-n rate conditions.
Doubly robust by construction: consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity score model is correctly specified, providing a safeguard against one misspecified nuisance.
Cross-fitting eliminates own-observation overfitting bias without sacrificing sample size, allowing any black-box ML learner (XGBoost, Lasso, neural nets) as plug-in for nuisance estimation.
weaknesses: Targets only a single global causal parameter (ATE or LATE); heterogeneous treatment effects require a further second-stage model (e.g., Causal Forest on residuals), adding complexity.
Highly sensitive to inclusion of endogenous 'bad controls': even a few post-treatment or collider variables among confounders cause substantial bias that Neyman-orthogonalization does not correct.
Requires strong overlap (positivity) and unconfoundedness; under limited overlap, propensity residuals blow up, inflating variance and breaking the root-n guarantees.
recommended_for: Policy evaluation in economics or medicine where the goal is a valid confidence interval around a single average treatment effect from observational data with 50+ confounders (e.g., wage effect of job training using administrative records).
A/B experiment analysis with imperfect randomization and many pre-treatment covariates, where residualization removes covariate imbalance and tightens standard errors without model-selection bias.
not_recommended_for: Problems requiring personalized treatment rules or individual-level effect estimates across many subgroups — DML alone produces a scalar estimate, not a CATE surface.

Settings where confounders cannot be pre-specified and automated variable selection is used from a mixed pool of controls, as endogenous regressors silently bias the estimate despite orthogonalization.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey, and Robins (2018) in 'Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Causal Parameters' (The Econometrics Journal, 21: C1–C68); the preprint circulated as arXiv:1608.00060 in 2016 and is among the most-cited works combining econometrics with modern ML, credited with reviving Neyman's 1959 orthogonality concept in a high-dimensional inference context.

children.name: Synthetic Control
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DiD (which assumes parallel trends across all control units) or ITS (which models a single unit's trend), Synthetic Control builds a counterfactual by solving a constrained optimization to find a convex combination of donor-pool units that replicates the treated unit's pre-intervention trajectory across multiple predictors simultaneously.
strengths: Transparent counterfactual: the synthetic unit is a named, inspectable weighted average of real donor units, making the comparison concrete and auditable.
Does not require a large number of treated units — valid for N=1 case studies (single country, state, or firm) where DiD is inapplicable.
Convex-hull constraint (weights sum to 1, each ≥ 0) prevents extrapolation beyond the observed donor space, bounding interpolation bias.
weaknesses: Requires a long, stable pre-intervention period (typically 10+ time points) to credibly fit donor weights; short pre-periods lead to overfitting.
Inference relies on permutation (placebo) tests over the donor pool, which have low power when the donor pool is small (fewer than ~20 units).
Sensitive to donor pool composition: a poorly chosen or contaminated donor pool (units also exposed to the intervention) invalidates the counterfactual.
recommended_for: Evaluating a policy applied to a single aggregate unit (e.g., one state's tax reform) with 15+ years of pre-treatment panel data on 20–50 comparable untreated units.
Cross-country or cross-market comparative case studies where randomization is impossible and the treated case is sui generis, requiring a data-driven composite control.
not_recommended_for: Settings where the treated unit lies outside the convex hull of donor units in covariate space — the method cannot extrapolate and will produce a poor pre-period fit.
High-frequency, noisy outcomes (daily stock returns, hourly sensor data) where pre-period volatility makes weight optimization unstable and placebo tests lose interpretability.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) to estimate the economic cost of terrorism in the Basque Country, the method was formalized and given its current optimization framework by Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, accumulating over 4,000 citations within a decade.
keywords: estimate impact of a policy or intervention
construct synthetic counterfactual from control units
what would have happened without the intervention

children.name: PSM (Propensity Score Matching)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DiD (which requires panel data and parallel trends) and IV (which requires a valid instrument uncorrelated with unmeasured confounders), PSM collapses all observed covariates into a single scalar — the conditional treatment probability — and matches treated to control units on that scalar alone, without exploiting time variation or external variation.
strengths: Reduces high-dimensional covariate adjustment to a 1-D scalar, making matching feasible when there are dozens of confounders that would cause the curse of dimensionality in direct covariate matching.

Balancing treated and control groups on the propensity score is provably sufficient to eliminate confounding from all included covariates (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983), without specifying an outcome model.

Transparent diagnostic: the standardized mean difference (SMD) before vs. after matching is a model-agnostic balance check that does not require access to outcome data, preserving the separation between design and analysis.
weaknesses: Cannot balance unobserved confounders — if any unmeasured variable jointly predicts treatment assignment and outcome, the ATT estimate remains biased regardless of how well the propensity score is estimated.
Matching discards unmatched treated units (and controls), reducing effective sample size, which increases variance and can introduce selection bias when overlap between groups is limited.

The propensity score itself must be estimated (usually via logistic regression), and misspecification of that model — wrong functional form, missing interactions, or collinearity — produces a biased score and poor balance.
recommended_for: Retrospective observational studies in epidemiology or economics where treatment was not randomized but a rich set of pre-treatment covariates (demographics, prior health measures, baseline outcomes) is recorded for both treated and untreated subjects.

Program evaluation with a large administrative dataset where the treatment group is small relative to a large control pool, allowing tight 1:k nearest-neighbor matching with a narrow caliper (e.g., 0.02 SD of the logit score) without depleting controls.
not_recommended_for: Settings with strong unmeasured confounding (e.g., patient self-selection based on unrecorded severity) where IV or DiD can exploit an exogenous source of variation to purge the bias that PSM cannot touch.

High-dimensional genetic or text data where hundreds of potential confounders make propensity score model specification unreliable; doubly-robust estimators (AIPW) or targeted learning (TMLE) are better suited because they combine outcome and propensity models with error-correction guarantees.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) in 'The Central Role of the Propensity Score in Observational Studies for Causal Effects' (Biometrika, 70(1):41-55), the paper proved the balancing property — that conditioning on the propensity score renders treatment assignment independent of all observed covariates — which gave theoretical justification for replacing multivariate matching with a single estimated probability.

children.name: IPW (Inverse Probability Weighting)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike meta-learners (S/T/X-learner) that directly model outcome functions, IPW re-weights observations by the inverse of the propensity score P(T=1|X) to create a pseudo-population where treatment assignment is independent of confounders, estimating the ATE without fitting a separate outcome model.
strengths: Non-parametric in the outcome model — correct propensity score estimation yields unbiased ATE even when the outcome-covariate relationship is complex or unknown.
Naturally handles multi-valued and time-varying treatments by extending weights to each treatment level or time point without re-specifying an outcome model.
Doubly robust when combined with outcome regression (AIPW): consistent if either the propensity model or the outcome model is correctly specified, not necessarily both.
weaknesses: Extreme weights when propensity scores are near 0 or 1 (near-violation of positivity) inflate variance sharply and can cause numerical instability.
Requires a correctly specified propensity score model — misspecification (wrong functional form or omitted confounders) produces biased ATE estimates.

Inefficient relative to doubly robust estimators in large samples; the Horvitz-Thompson estimator in particular has higher variance than regression-adjusted alternatives when the outcome model is available.
recommended_for: Observational studies with binary treatment and rich covariate data where the selection-into-treatment mechanism is well understood and can be modeled (e.g., clinical database studies with documented eligibility criteria).
Settings requiring marginal (population-level) treatment effect estimates across the full covariate distribution, such as policy evaluation where the target population differs from the treated group.
